# Conclusions

Overall, this project suggests that data centers are not simply built in isolated rural areas, but are instead closely associated with more urban and populous counties. Our clustering results showed a clear difference between counties with very few data centers and counties with many, even when the clustering model had no direct access to data center counts. At the same time, the measurable difference-in-differences effects were concentrated in the more rural cluster, suggesting that data center development may have a more noticeable effect in smaller local economies than in larger urban ones.

Our difference-in-differences results point to a mixed local economic impact. Higher in-county and nearby data center exposure was associated with lower personal income and declines in trade and transportation, industrial, and primary-industry employment, but also with lower unemployment, increased construction activity, and lower $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ air pollution in certain cases. These patterns suggest that data centers bring real local trade-offs rather than uniform economic benefits or downsides.

By combining public NAICS 518 data with a reproducible county-level time-series pipeline, spatial exposure measures, and staggered DiD models, this project provides an accessible framework for studying those trade-offs across the contiguous United States. At the same time, NAICS 518 is an imperfect proxy for data centers because it does not provide information on individual facilities’ geographic coordinates or size. Taken together, these findings suggest that data centers should not be expected to produce uniform local outcomes, as their economic and environmental impacts appear to vary with the characteristic of the communities in which they are located.
